walkthroughs.body_html:
Inorganic Chemistry — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Inorganic Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Inorganic Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series share:
options: The same molecular mass
The same functional group and general formula
The same boiling point
The same number of isomers

mcqs.q: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
options: Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so electrons are held more tightly.
Atoms get bigger across a period, making electrons easier to add but harder to remove.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.

mcqs.q: Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
